x.KJV: A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver him, yet thou must do it again.

nt: **One great of heat** represents a type of person in general, not one particular person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a more natural expression. Alternate translation: [Any person great of heat]

**One great of heat** refers to someone who is extremely angry. Here, **heat** refers to anger, which causes the angry person’s body to become hot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar use of **heat** in [6:34](../06/34.md). Alternate translation: [An extremely angry person]

Here Solomon speaks of a person experiencing the consequences for what happens when he gets angry as if those consequences were a **fine** that he **lifts up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [must experience the consequences]

Here Solomon implies that this **fine** is for something bad that the extremely angry person has done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [a fine for what he does when he is angry]

Solomon is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a clause would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [if you rescue him from paying a fine] or [if you rescue him from trouble]

x.ASV: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, That thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.
x.Darby: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.
x.KJV: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.
x.YLT: Hear counsel and receive instruction, So that thou art wise in thy latter end.

nt: See how you translated the abstract nouns **counsel** in [1:25](../01/25.md) and **instruction** in [1:2](../01/02.md).

Here, **so that** indicates that what follows is the purpose for obeying the commands in the previous clause. Use the most natural way in your language to express a purpose. Alternate translation: [for the purpose of becoming wise]

This could refer to: (1) the future in general. Alternate translation: [in the future] or [after you are taught]; (2) the time near the end of one’s life. Alternate translation: [when your life is almost over]

x.ASV: There are many devices in a man’s heart; But the counsel of Jehovah, that shall stand.
x.Darby: Many are the thoughts in a man's heart, but the counsel of Jehovah, that doth stand.
x.KJV: There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.
x.YLT: Many are the purposes in a man's heart, And the counsel of Jehovah it standeth.

nt: Here Solomon speaks of **the plans** that a person thinks about as if they were objects located **in** that person’s **heart**. Alternate translation: [are the plans thought about by]
Although **man** is masculine, here it refers to any person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [a person]

Here Solomon is using the possessive form to describe the **counsel** that **Yahweh** gives. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a different expression. Alternate translation: [but the counsel that Yahweh gives]
See how you translated the abstract noun **counsel** in the previous verse.

Here Solomon refers to **counsel** that is successful as if it were a person who could **stand**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. See how you translated the same phrase in [15:22](../15/22.md). Alternate translation: [it will be successful]

x.ASV: That which maketh a man to be desired is his kindness; And a poor man is better than a liar.
x.Darby: The charm of a man is his kindness; and a poor [man] is better than a liar.
x.KJV: The desire of a man is his kindness: and a poor man is better than a liar.
x.YLT: The desirableness of a man is his kindness, And better is the poor than a liar.

nt: This phrase could mean: (1) what **a man** desires for himself. Alternate translation: [What a man desires] or (2) what others desire **a man** to be like. Alternate translation: [What people desire in a man]

Here, **a man**, **his**, **one who is poor**, and **a man of lying** refer to types of people in general, not specific people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use more natural expressions. Alternate translation: [a person is that person’s covenant faithfulness … is a person who is poor than a person of lying]
See how you translated the abstract noun **covenant faithfulness** in [3:3](../03/03.md).

Here Solomon is using the possessive form to describe a **man** who is characterized by **lying**. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a different expression. Alternate translation: [than a man characterized by lying] or [than a liar]

x.ASV: The fear of Jehovah tendeth to life; And he that hath it shall abide satisfied; He shall not be visited with evil.
x.Darby: The fear of Jehovah [tendeth] to life, and he [that hath it] shall rest satisfied without being visited with evil.
x.KJV: The fear of the Lord tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil.
x.YLT: The fear of Jehovah is to life, And satisfied he remaineth--he is not charged with evil.

nt: See how you translated this phrase in [1:7](../01/07.md).
See how you translated this phrase in [10:16](../10/16.md).

The phrase **stay overnight** here is an idiom that refers to resting or sleeping. The idea is that the person who fears Yahweh will have satisfying rest through the night. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and this person will rest satisfied]

Solomon is using the adjective **satisfied** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the satisfied person]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [evil will not visit him]

Here Solomon speaks of a person experiencing **evil** as if **evil** were a person who could visit him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will not experience evil]

Here, **evil** refers to trouble that someone might experience as a result of **evil**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [trouble]

x.ASV: The sluggard burieth his hand in the dish, And will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.
x.Darby: A sluggard burieth his hand in the dish, and will not even bring it to his mouth again.
x.KJV: A slothful man hideth his hand in his bosom, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.
x.YLT: The slothful hath hidden his hand in a dish, Even unto his mouth he bringeth it not back.

nt: **A lazy one**, **his**, and **he** refer to a type of person in general, not a specific person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use more natural expressions. See how you translated **A lazy one** in [10:26](../10/26.md). Alternate translation: [Any lazy one … that person’s hand … that person will not even return it to that person’s own mouth]

In Solomon’s culture, people usually ate with their hands and put their hands **in a dish** in order to pick up food and eat it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [puts his hand in the dish in order to pick up food]

Here Solomon implies that **A lazy one** does not **return** his hand **to his mouth** because he is too lazy to do so. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [but he is too lazy to even bring his hand up to his mouth to feed himself]

x.ASV: Smite a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; And reprove one that hath understanding, and he will understand knowledge.
x.Darby: Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware; reprove the intelligent, and he will understand knowledge.
x.KJV: Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware: and reprove one that hath understanding, and he will understand knowledge.
x.YLT: A scorner smite, and the simple acts prudently, And give reproof to the intelligent, He understandeth knowledge.

nt: Solomon assumes that his readers will understand that **Strike** refers to a way of punishing **a mocker**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Punish a mocker by striking him]

Alternate translation: [any mocker and any naive one … any understanding one—that person will understand]

You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and a naive one will see this happen and become prudent]
See how you translated the abstract noun **knowledge** in [1:4](../01/04.md).

x.KJV: He that wasteth his father, and chaseth away his mother, is a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach.
x.YLT: Whoso is spoiling a father causeth a mother to flee, A son causing shame, and bringing confusion.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **violence**, **shame**, and **embarrassment**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. **One who does violence** here refers to this type of person in general, not a specific person. If it would be helpful, you could use a more natural expression in your language. Alternate translation: [Any person who does violence]

Although **son** is masculine, Solomon is using those words in a generic sense that could refer to either a male or female child. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a phrase that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [is a child]

x.ASV: Cease, my son, to hear instruction Only to err from the words of knowledge.
x.Darby: Cease, my son, to hear the instruction which causeth to stray from the words of knowledge.
x.KJV: Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge.
x.YLT: Cease, my son, to hear instruction--To err from sayings of knowledge.

nt: See how you translated the same use of this phrase in [1:8](../01/08.md).

Here Solomon is using an imperative sentence to introduce a condition. He is pointing out that if his son ceases to hear instruction, the result will be a life without knowledge. If a speaker of your language would not use an imperative to introduce a condition, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if you cease to hear instruction, you will stray from the words of knowledge] or [do not cease to hear instruction, and you will not stray from the words of knowledge]
See how you translated the abstract noun **instruction** in [1:2](../01/02.md).
See how you translated the abstract noun **knowledge** in [1:4](../01/04.md).

Here, **to** indicates that what follows is the purpose of doing what was stated in the previous clause. Use the most natural way in your language to indicate that this is the ironic purpose of refusing to hear instruction. Alternate translation: [in order to stray] or [and then you will be far]

Here Solomon refers to a person straying or wandering from the **words of knowledge** to mean that the person is no longer heeding those **words**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to stop accepting the words of knowledge]

Here Solomon is using the possessive form to describe **words** that are characterized by **knowledge**. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a different expression. Alternate translation: [from the words that give knowledge]
See how you translated the similar use of **words** in [1:23](../01/23.md). Alternate translation: [from the sayings of] or [from the messages of]
